commits.pr_title: [Model Loader] Find safetensors shards listed in a subdirectory
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Lets the default loader find safetensors shards that `model.safetensors.index.json` lists in a subdirectory. NVIDIA's FP4-Local checkpoints keep shards under `tensors/`: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local has all 21 there, and GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local has one there next to 41 shards in the repo root. The loader only globs the root, so on main the first finds no weights and the second fails the index check with `Weight files referenced in index but missing`.

Split out of #64312, which needs this to load either checkpoint from the Hub.

## Claims

- When the index is present, `_prepare_weights` and `hash_checkpoint` use its shard list directly, without walking subdirectories. `filter_duplicate_safetensors_files` returns that list through a new helper and still raises when a listed file is missing. The helper also raises when the index lists a file outside the model folder, like `../other.safetensors` or an absolute path, which the old check rejected as missing. Without an index, nested files are ignored as before.
- A Hub snapshot fetches the index only when it isn't there yet: with several root shards, as before, and with no root shards when a subdirectory holds safetensors files. Single-file and `.bin`-only repos make no extra request. A snapshot with one root shard next to nested ones still needs the index from the download.
- `drop_checkpoint_cache` also drops the page cache for the listed shards that exist. If it can't read the index, it logs a warning and still handles the root files.
- Sources with explicit allow patterns don't change.

## Validation

On CPU, main (`f3f0a01424`) plus this PR:

```text
pytest tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_filter_duplicate_safetensors.py \
  tests/model_executor/test_weight_utils.py \
  tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_registry.py   # 88 passed, 1 skipped (needs a GPU)
pre-commit run --files <changed files>                 # passed
```

The loader test covers a Hub snapshot with two shards only under `tensors/`, one with two root shards and one under `tensors/`, a `.bin`-only one, and a local directory with its shard under `tensors/`. The `drop_checkpoint_cache` test adds a shard under `tensors/` and a broken index. On main, the three nested loader cases and the nested `drop_checkpoint_cache` case fail.

On a local copy of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local with the Hub layout, `_prepare_weights` returns exactly the 21 shards the index lists and `hash_checkpoint` returns a key. On the same copy, main's `_prepare_weights` raises `Cannot find any model weights` and its `hash_checkpoint` raises `Weight files referenced in index but missing`.

commits.pr_title: [Perf][Attention] Split only the sliding window into Triton split-K decode segments
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

In the Triton split-K (3D) decode path of `kernel_unified_attention`, the segments split the
whole sequence, so with a sliding window only 1-2 segments overlap the window once
`seq_len >> window`, and they walk it serially. This PR splits only the window's tiles into the
segments. Sliding-window decode then costs the same at any context length instead of growing
linearly. Complementary to #60418 (now merged), which made TRITON_ATTN the default on RDNA and
raised the gfx1201 split-K segment count; interacts with #56148 (multi-query split-K), see
Details.

## Claims

- **Per sliding-window layer, decode on TRITON_ATTN:** the cost no longer grows with context.
  On current `main` (with #60418) on an AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700, window 2048, cold L2:
  - batch 1: 1.46× at 12K, 2.7× at 32K, 4.8× at 64K, 8.7× at 128K tokens;
  - batch 4: 2.2× at 12K, 5.3× at 32K, ~10× at ≥ 64K.
  - With the default 16 segments (the launch CDNA and NVIDIA take; measured on the R9700 with
    the RDNA tuning disabled): 4.3× at 12K and ~11× at 32K for batch 1; 1.07-3.85× for batch 16
    from 4K to 32K; no regression at any batch size, including 64.
- **gpt-oss-20b shape** (window 128, attention sinks): correct with sinks; 1.3-1.5× per
  sliding-window layer at ≥ 4K tokens, batch 1-4.
- **End to end, Muse Glimmer 30B, TP=4 on 4× R9700, `--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN`, measured
  before #60418:** TPOT −1.2% at 4K and −4.9% at 12K context (c=1), unchanged below the window,
  GSM8K unchanged. With #60418 the batch-1 gain at 12K is smaller (see Validation).
- **No change where the window does not bound the keys or the path differs:**
  - full attention, context ≤ window (≤ 1% overhead there, see Details);
  - the 2D path, spec-decode verify (`max_seqlen_q > 1`);
  - chunked-local, multimodal-prefix, R-SWA and per-sequence-causal masks.
- **Tests:** two new tests guard that the window layout is actually used and is correct; the
  existing numerical test would not notice it silently turning off.

## Validation

**Kernel microbenchmark on current `main`.** Setup: R9700 (gfx1201), 8 q / 1 KV heads, head 128,
block 16, bf16, window 2048. With #60418 the split-K segment count follows the batch (128 / 64 /
32 segments at batch 1 / 2 / 4, confirmed in the launch grids). Statistic: rocprofv3
kernel-duration median of 200 dispatches per case, CUDA-graph replay, baseline
(`window_aware_segments=False`) and change interleaved in one process and run in both orders,
512 MB read-only buffer pass before every call to evict the caches. Values are
`kernel_unified_attention` + `reduce_segments`:

| context | batch 1 before → after | batch 2 | batch 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| ≤ 2K | 0.99-1.00× | 0.99-1.00× | 0.99× |
| 4K | 7.4 → 7.1 µs (1.05×) | 9.2 → 8.6 µs (1.06×) | 12.9 → 11.8 µs (1.09×) |
| 8K | 8.8 → 7.1 µs (1.23×) | 12.4 → 8.6 µs (1.43×) | 19.5 → 11.8 µs (1.65×) |
| 12K | 10.3 → 7.1 µs (1.46×) | 15.7 → 8.6 µs (1.82×) | 26.4 → 11.8 µs (2.23×) |
| 32K | 19.4 → 7.2 µs (2.72×) | 33.6 → 8.7 µs (3.87×) | 62.9 → 11.9 µs (5.29×) |
| 64K | 33.4 → 7.0 µs (4.75×) | 61.7 → 8.6 µs (7.18×) | 118.8 → 11.9 µs (10.0×) |
| 128K | 61.7 → 7.1 µs (8.74×) | 119.0 → 8.6 µs (13.8×) | 118.9 → 11.8 µs (10.1×) |

After the change the layer costs the same at every context ≥ the window. Without it the cost grows
until context = segments × window (256K at batch 1 with 128 segments). Full-attention control
(identical kernel under both labels): 0.999-1.004.

<details>
<summary>Batch 16, gpt-oss-20b shape, and the default 16-segment launch (CDNA/NVIDIA path)</summary>

Current `main`, window 2048, batch 16 (8 segments): 1.18× at 4K, 2.01× at 8K, 2.91× at 12K,
3.82× at 32K.

Current `main`, gpt-oss-20b per-GPU shape (64 q / 8 KV heads, head 64, window 128, sinks; 16
segments), batch 1 / 2 / 4: 1.15-1.19× at 1K, 1.34-1.54× from 4K to 128K.

Default 16-segment launch on current `main` (the path CDNA and NVIDIA take; on the R9700 with
#60418's RDNA launch tuning disabled, kernels unchanged), window 2048, same method:

| context | batch 1 | batch 4 | batch 16 | batch 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ≤ 2K | 1.00× | 0.99-1.00× | 1.00× | 1.00× |
| 4K | 18.3 → 11.1 µs (1.65×) | 1.54× | 34.8 → 32.6 µs (1.07×) | 1.01× |
| 8K | 33.0 → 11.1 µs (2.98×) | 2.65× | 41.5 → 32.6 µs (1.27×) | 1.00× |
| 12K | 47.7 → 11.0 µs (4.33×) | 3.84× | 54.0 → 32.7 µs (1.65×) | – |
| 32K | 122.5 → 11.1 µs (11.1×) | 9.79× | 125.6 → 32.6 µs (3.85×) | – |

Full-attention control: 0.997-1.002.

</details>

**End to end (measured before #60418).** Muse Glimmer 30B, TP=4 on 4× R9700, TRITON_ATTN, best
stock config, 3 interleaved rounds, round-to-round spread ≤ 0.02 ms at c=1. Measured on the first
revision of this change (identical kernel logic), ported onto vLLM `98dff2a81`:

| workload | TPOT before → after | output tok/s |
|---|---|---|
| multimodal 512 → 128, c=1 (under the window) | 27.18 → 27.13 ms | 33.94 → 34.00 |
| text 4K → 512, c=1 | 27.95 → 27.60 ms (−1.2%) | 33.16 → 33.55 |
| text 12K → 512, c=1 | 29.42 → 27.99 ms (−4.9%) | 27.70 → 28.85 |

On current `main`, #60418's larger segment count already removes most of the batch-1 cost at
12K, so the expected end-to-end gain there is smaller (~0.1 ms per token from the kernel numbers
above); it remains larger at longer contexts and at c=2-4.

GSM8K 25-shot for Muse Glimmer (prompts 3.3K-4.9K tokens, all beyond the window): flexible-extract
0.9363 → 0.9348, strict-match 0.9371 → 0.9356 (± 0.0067); 99.2% identical answers.

**gpt-oss-20b serving** (before #60418; TP=1 on one R9700, default TRITON_ATTN): sliding-window
attention per call 10.34 → 4.96 µs (rocprofv3, 8K, c=4); TPOT −0.1 … −0.3% at c=1. The gain is
small because the 128-token window spans only 8-9 tiles and attention is a minor part of the MoE
step. Greedy outputs are deterministic per variant and diverge only at near-ties.

**Correctness and tests (gfx1201, on the PR head merged with current `main`):**

```bash
pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_triton_unified_attention.py \
       tests/kernels/attention/test_triton_unified_attention_diffkv.py \
       tests/kernels/attention/test_mixed_causal_attn.py \
       tests/v1/attention/test_triton_attn_segments.py \
       tests/quantization/test_per_token_kv_cache.py
```

- 2251 passed, 10 skipped, 0 failed.
- Differential check, new vs old split vs fp32 reference: GQA 1/5/8, windows 8/16/17/64/2048, with
  and without attention sinks, contexts at every window/tile edge. Error vs fp32 is unchanged;
  new vs old differ by ≤ 0.5 bf16 ulp.
- The tests were checked by seeding one bug at a time ("fails" = the test caught the bug,
  "passes" = it did not). Every bug is caught by at least one test; the first and third would
  pass the numerical test alone:

  | seeded bug | `test_window_aware_segments_gate` | `test_split_k_window_segment_tile_ranges` | `test_triton_unified_attn_window_aware_segments` (numerical) |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | gate silently off | fails | passes | passes |
  | `reduce_segments` without the flag | fails | passes | fails |
  | wrong active-segment count | passes | fails | passes |
  | window start off by one tile | passes | fails | fails |

**CI.** The tests live in `tests/kernels/attention`, which runs in the Buildkite kernel shards
(NVIDIA and MI300/MI355). RDNA (gfx1201) is not in CI; the results above were collected locally.

## Details

**Root cause.** `tiles_per_segment = cdiv(seq_len, NUM_SEGMENTS * TILE_SIZE)` lays the segments
over `[0, seq_len)`. `compute_tile_loop_bounds` then intersects each segment with the window. For
`seq_len >> window` the window falls into one or two segments, each walking up to
`min(window, seq_len / NUM_SEGMENTS)` tokens serially, while the other segments exit. The cost
therefore grows with context until `seq_len = NUM_SEGMENTS × window`.

**Change.**

- `split_k_segment_layout()` (new, `triton_attention_helpers.py`) returns
  `(base_tile, tiles_per_segment, num_active)`. With `WINDOW_SEGMENTS` the segments cover the
  decode query's window tiles `[⌊max(L−W,0)/T⌋, ⌈L/T⌉)`; otherwise the whole sequence, with the
  same values as before. Both `kernel_unified_attention` and `reduce_segments` call it, so they
  always agree on which segments are active.
- `compute_tile_loop_bounds()` gets an optional `segm_base_tile_or_0` (default 0); other callers
  are unchanged. The kernel's early exit becomes `segm_idx >= num_active`, which is equivalent to
  the previous condition.
- The launcher enables `WINDOW_SEGMENTS` only for the 3D path with `max_seqlen_q == 1`, causal,
  and a plain sliding window: not chunked-local, mm-prefix, R-SWA or per-sequence causal. In
  those cases the window does not bound the keys of a single decode query, or (spec-decode
  verify, enabled in 3D by #56148) there are several queries per sequence. The gate is evaluated
  after the RDNA launch tuning from #60418, so both kernels receive the same flag, segment count
  and tile size. `reduce_segments` gets `SLIDING_WINDOW` only when the flag is on, to avoid
  compiling a reduce variant per window size.
- `window_aware_segments: bool = True` on `unified_attention()` forces the old split. The new
  tests and the A/B benchmark use it.

**Tradeoffs and limitations.**

- Up to ~1% slower on SWA layers when the context is shorter than the window: the window-range
  arithmetic runs even when the window covers everything (≈ 0.05 µs of ~5 µs).
- No benefit:
  - for spec-decode verify steps (`max_seqlen_q > 1`), which keep the whole-sequence split; a
    short-query extension is possible as a follow-up;
  - for multimodal-prefix models with an image in the batch (`mm_prefix_range` is batch-wide);
  - for the int4 per-token-head KV cache (separate kernel);
  - above the 3D threshold (2D path);
  - on backends other than TRITON_ATTN.
- On ROCm, TRITON_ATTN is the default on gfx1201/gfx1100 since #60418; elsewhere plain-SWA models
  default to ROCM_ATTN unless TRITON_ATTN is selected. Models with sinks (gpt-oss) and mm-prefix
  models already land on TRITON_ATTN.
- No CPU/GPU synchronization is added: the gate uses only host-side launcher arguments.
- Complexity: +80 / −9 lines outside tests.

---

<details>
<summary> Pull Request Checklist </summary>

- [x] I used vLLM's `/pr-checklist` skill. (Mandatory for agents, optional for humans).
- [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR.

- [ ] **Design Fit:** Minimizes impact on core components, reuses existing functionality, and justifies added complexity.
- [ ] **Testing and Validation:** Validates the change and ensures any added tests are meaningful and reliable, with CI coverage or documented CI resource constraints and validation performed outside CI.
- [ ] **Code Quality and Style:** Keeps code and comments clear and concise, and updates relevant documentation and examples.
- [ ] **Pull Request Contents:** Includes a brief summary and relevant links, supports claims with evidence, explains root causes and implementation trade-offs, and follows the contributing guide.
</details>

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][RDNA][Perf] W4A16: fused scale/zero-point carrier for Triton prefill
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

For asymmetric fp16 W4A16 layers on gfx1151 (Strix Halo), `RDNAHybridW4A16LinearKernel` now trades a little weight memory for faster prefill. At load time, each per-group scale and zero-point is packed into one int32 "carrier". The packed fp16 Triton prefill dequant (#60644) then does one load per (n, group) and a single `v_pk_fma_f16` per pair. Before, it did a scale load, a packed zero-point gather, and a subtract-then-multiply. With the cheaper dequant, asymmetric layers take the packed path from M > 192 (M > 128 when N ≥ 4K) instead of M > 256.

Builds on #60644. Not a duplicate: no open PR adds a scale/zero-point carrier or changes the asymmetric prefill cutoff. #61193 also speeds up gfx1151 prefill, but at M ≥ 4096 by dequantizing to a dense matmul; the two are complementary but touch the same file.

## Claims

- **Batch-1 prefill up to 18% faster end to end.** Qwen3-8B (asymmetric g128): −18.4% at 224 prompt tokens, −17.3% at 256. Qwen3-1.7B (asymmetric g64): −12.1% at 224, −12.4% at 256. No change at 128 tokens, and within ±1.8% from 320 tokens up.
- **No regression at batch 128 and 256** (outputs 1 and 128): Qwen3-8B is 3–11% faster, Qwen3-1.7B 1–5%.
- **Kernel** (geomean over 12 Qwen3 shapes, g128 and g64): 15–18% faster at M 193–256, 4–5% at M 129–192, 1–3% at M 257–4096. At M = 8192, summed over each model's four layers: 12% faster on Qwen3-8B, 5% on Qwen3-1.7B.
- **Memory cost:** 8/G of the int4 weight bytes (6.25% at g128, 12.5% at g64). Measured KV cache is 0.16–0.20% smaller.
- **Accuracy:** GSM8K within one question on both models. Symmetric output is bit-identical to main.
- **Unchanged:** symmetric layers, bf16, g32 (bit-identical to main), the skinny HIP decode path, and every GPU other than gfx1151.

## Validation

gfx1151 (Radeon 8060S, 20 CUs), torch 2.13.0+rocm10.2.0a20260923, Triton 3.8.0. End-to-end runs compare main at `4b47db922b` with this PR rebased on it. Kernel runs compare against main at `0fddee1f58`; `rdna_hybrid_w4a16.py` is identical on both. Each comparison runs both arms on one build, interleaved, alternating which arm goes first per rep.

### End to end: batch-1 prefill latency

This command for each prompt length, 8 runs per arm on main and on this PR. Cells are the median over runs; `~` marks overlapping run ranges.

```
vllm bench latency --model RedHatAI/Qwen3-8B-quantized.w4a16 --dtype float16 \
    --max-model-len 4096 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 256 \
    --no-enable-prefix-caching --seed 0 \
    --batch-size 1 --input-len 224 --output-len 1 \
    --num-iters-warmup 3 --num-iters 15
```

| prompt tokens | Qwen3-8B main → PR (ms) | change | Qwen3-1.7B main → PR (ms) | change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 93.7 → 93.6 | −0.1% ~ | 26.3 → 25.2 | −4.2% ~ |
| 160 | 141.4 → 131.3 | **−7.2%** | 36.3 → 34.2 | −5.6% ~ |
| 192 | 142.5 → 134.4 | **−5.7%** | 36.8 → 34.4 | −6.5% ~ |
| 224 | 166.4 → 135.9 | **−18.4%** | 41.5 → 36.4 | **−12.1%** |
| 256 | 168.0 → 138.9 | **−17.3%** | 42.3 → 37.0 | **−12.4%** |
| 320 | 195.4 → 193.1 | −1.2% ~ | 53.8 → 53.4 | −0.8% ~ |
| 384 | 200.9 → 197.4 | −1.8% ~ | 55.0 → 55.4 | +0.8% ~ |
| 512 | 271.6 → 268.9 | −1.0% ~ | 67.7 → 67.0 | −1.0% ~ |
| 1024 | 535.3 → 535.0 | −0.0% ~ | 134.5 → 133.1 | −1.1% ~ |
| 2048 | 1132.9 → 1117.9 | −1.3% | 286.5 → 284.3 | −0.8% ~ |

Control: Qwen3-4B-quantized.w4a16 (symmetric) at 128 / 256 / 512 / 2048 tokens, +0.3% / −0.0% / −0.8% / +0.1%, all overlapping.

### End to end: batch 128 and 256

The same command with `--batch-size 128|256 --input-len 128|512 --output-len 1|128 --num-iters-warmup 1 --num-iters 3`, 3 runs per arm. No cell's run ranges overlap.

| batch | prompt | output | Qwen3-8B main → PR (s) | change | Qwen3-1.7B main → PR (s) | change |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 128 | 1 | 9.74 → 8.89 | **−8.8%** | 2.33 → 2.25 | −3.5% |
| 128 | 128 | 128 | 26.28 → 25.51 | −2.9% | 7.16 → 7.07 | −1.2% |
| 128 | 512 | 1 | 39.35 → 35.85 | **−8.9%** | 9.27 → 8.87 | −4.4% |
| 128 | 512 | 128 | 63.04 → 59.98 | −4.9% | 17.35 → 16.98 | −2.1% |
| 256 | 128 | 1 | 19.53 → 17.80 | **−8.8%** | 4.68 → 4.49 | −4.0% |
| 256 | 128 | 128 | 50.22 → 44.83 | **−10.7%** | 13.66 → 12.99 | −4.9% |
| 256 | 512 | 1 | 78.98 → 72.09 | **−8.7%** | 18.51 → 17.88 | −3.4% |
| 256 | 512 | 128 | 123.42 → 113.62 | **−7.9%** | 34.09 → 32.93 | −3.4% |

Prefill at these batch sizes runs in 8192-token chunks, so its GEMMs are at M = 8192. There the PR's kernels take 0.88× main's time on Qwen3-8B and 0.95× on Qwen3-1.7B, summed over each model's four layers. Decode at batch 256 runs at M = 256 and takes the carrier path; decode at batch 128 (M = 128) is unchanged.

### Kernel

`_rdna_hybrid_w4a16_apply_impl` timed with `triton.testing.do_bench`, which flushes cache between reps so weights come from DRAM. 3 reps, median over reps. Shapes: qkv/o/gate_up/down of Qwen3-8B, 4B and 1.7B. Time ratio PR / main, < 1 is faster:

| M | 128 | 129 | 160 | 192 | 193 | 224 | 256 | 257 | 384 | 512 | 1024 | 2048 | 4096 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| g128 geomean | 1.00 | 0.95 | 0.96 | 0.96 | 0.82 | 0.83 | 0.84 | 0.99 | 0.99 | 0.99 | 0.98 | 0.99 | 0.97 |
| g64 geomean | 1.00 | 0.96 | 0.96 | 0.96 | 0.83 | 0.84 | 0.85 | 0.99 | 0.98 | 0.98 | 0.98 | 0.98 | 0.97 |
| g128 best / worst shape | 1.00 / 1.01 | 0.82 / 1.01 | 0.82 / 1.01 | 0.83 / 1.00 | 0.59 / 1.16 | 0.61 / 1.18 | 0.63 / 1.23 | 0.95 / 1.01 | 0.95 / 1.03 | 0.92 / 1.03 | 0.92 / 1.04 | 0.97 / 1.02 | 0.95 / 0.99 |

The one regression is Qwen3-4B down_proj (N=2560, K=9728) at M 193–256: 1.16–1.24× at g128 and g64. Summed over Qwen3-4B's four layers, asymmetric is still 0.85–0.89× main at g128 (0.87–0.91× at g64) at those M. I did not run asymmetric Qwen3-4B end to end.

At M = 8192, the chunk size at large batch, per layer (g128 Qwen3-8B / g64 Qwen3-1.7B, 3 reps): qkv 0.91 / 0.96, o 0.90 / 0.99, gate_up 0.91 / 0.95, down 0.81 / 0.91.

g32 (no carrier) vs main: bit-identical output in 252/252 cells, time ratio 0.99–1.00 geomean at every M.

### Accuracy

- GSM8K 5-shot, 500 questions, fp16, `tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py` against `vllm serve`, #60644 head → this change: Qwen3-8B 0.884 → 0.882, Qwen3-1.7B 0.654 → 0.652. Each is one question.
- Relative error vs an fp32 dequantize-then-matmul reference: 3.98e-4 with the carrier vs 2.86e-4 without, because `bias_eff` is rounded to fp16.
- Symmetric output is bit-identical to main (168/168 cells).

### Tests

```
pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_rdna_hybrid_w4a16.py \
       tests/kernels/quantization/test_w4a16_kernel_selection.py
338 passed, 8 skipped (bf16 carrier cases) on gfx1151
```

New or updated tests:
- prefill GEMM vs the fp32 oracle in symmetric, zero-point and carrier modes;
- `reload_weights` rebuilds the carrier in its original storage.

CI coverage: the AMD quantization-kernels step runs these files on gfx942. There both carrier tests skip, because the GEMM test needs gfx11/gfx12 and the reload test needs gfx1151, so the carrier path is validated on gfx1151 outside CI (above).

### Reproduce

- Kernel: `python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_rdna_hybrid_w4a16_gemm.py --models RedHatAI/Qwen3-8B-quantized.w4a16 --group-size 128`. Compare the `hybrid-w4a16-zp` and `hybrid-w4a16-scale-zp` providers.

## Details

**Carrier layout.** `[N, K//G]` int32: low 16 bits are the fp16 scale, high 16 bits are fp16 `bias_eff = -zp * scale`. Dequant is `(b_raw - 1024) * scale + bias_eff` on the magic-constant unpack from #60644. The output is not bit-identical to the zero-point path, because `bias_eff` is rounded to fp16 and fused into an FMA (see Accuracy).

**Where it is built.** Only asymmetric layers with fp16 scales, g ≥ 64, on gfx1151, the only place the packed dequant runs. On the scalar dequant (fp16 at small M, all bf16) the carrier measured about 1% slower on average with some cells 10–20% slower, since that path is VALU-issue-bound. It is a `Parameter`, so layerwise `reload_weights` recomputes it and copies it into its original storage. A non-persistent buffer would keep its stale value; the new reload test fails with one.

**Why the cutoffs.** Packed tiles with the carrier vs the scalar ladder (time ratio, < 1 favors the carrier), geomean over shapes. Shapes include synthetic K=4096 with N = 3K, 4K, 5K, since no real shape falls between N/K 2.4 and 6.

| g128 | 64 | 96 | 128 | 129 | 160 | 192 | 193 | 224 | 256 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| N < 4K (10 shapes) | 1.21 | 1.06 | 1.08 | 1.06 | 1.05 | 1.05 | 0.80 | 0.81 | 0.82 |
| N ≥ 4K (5 shapes) | 1.52 | 1.18 | 1.15 | 0.82 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0.85 |

- M ≤ 128: the packed path loses on every shape, so it is unchanged.
- M 129–192: N ≥ 4K wins by 16–18%, including the synthetic N = 4K and 5K shapes.
- M > 192: everything wins. The step at 193 is the scalar ladder's 64-row tiles needing a fourth M-tile.
- From M 129 up, g64 matches g128 within 0.02.
- The `N ≥ 4K` rule is conservative: synthetic N = 3K gains 7% at M 129–192 and Qwen3 qkv shapes (N ≥ 6144, N/K 1.5–2.4) gain 6–11%. Every other shape with N ≤ 4096 loses there except Qwen3-4B o_proj (+2–3%). `N > 4096` would fit these 15 shapes better, but I kept the rule that holds without tuning to them.

**Why not g32.** At g32 the carrier would be 12–15% faster than main at M 193–256. From M 257, where main uses the zero-point gather, it is −3% to +2% against it (worst shape +20%), and it costs 25% of the int4 weight bytes. g32 keeps main's path: packed zero-point gather from M > 256.

**Memory.** Decode (`wvSplitK_int4_g`, #57199) still reads the original scales and zero-points, so the carrier is an extra copy. If decode read the carrier instead, those copies could be dropped; that is left for a follow-up.

**Interactions.**
- #60710's opt-in dense weight cache already covers M ≥ 256 when enabled, so with it on the carrier matters only at M 129–256.
- #52637 (open) also changes `process_weights_after_loading` in this file.
- #61193 (open) also edits the prefill dispatch in `rdna_hybrid_w4a16.py`.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for the code, tests, benchmarks and this description. I reviewed every changed line and ran the tests and benchmarks above.

commits.pr_title: [Doc] Sleep mode: free a KV connector's host memory with Mooncake standalone-store
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Document how to free a KV connector's host memory while a colocated engine sleeps. Resetting the connector's cache does not return its host memory: `MooncakeStoreConnector` in its default `embedded` mode keeps its pool share inside each rank for the engine's lifetime. With `standalone-store`, the pool lives in the external `mooncake_client`, which can be stopped while vLLM sleeps and started again before serving resumes. The section sits in the sleep mode docs next to "Keep the KV connector cache" and notes that the pool's KV cache is lost, so later lookups miss and recompute. The Mooncake store docs link to it.

## Test Plan

Docs only. Checked the documented steps on one GB300 GPU (vLLM nightly 153dc0464, Mooncake 0.3.14, RDMA, Qwen3-0.6B, `standalone-store`, default connector options):

1. Sleep (level 1), stop `mooncake_client`: vLLM stays up, `/health` 200.
2. Start `mooncake_client` at the same address, wake, send a prompt that hit the store before: HTTP 200, `external_prefix_cache_hits` unchanged (miss, recomputed), no errors.
3. Requests while `mooncake_client` is down: HTTP 200 as misses; store puts only log warnings.
4. Host used memory drops by the client's RSS (~5 GiB) when it stops and returns when it restarts.

commits.pr_title: [Build] Bump humming-kernels to 0.1.20
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Bump `humming-kernels` from 0.1.19 to 0.1.20 ([release notes](https://github.com/vllm-project/humming/releases/tag/v0.1.20)).

## Claims

Notable changes since 0.1.19:

**Fixes**

- Weight scale groups that are not a power of two are split instead of mishandled (vllm-project/humming#203; related to #66437).
- Fused shards and N padding no longer shrink the E8M0 scale range (vllm-project/humming#193).
- Weight dequantization keeps 64-bit element counts (vllm-project/humming#196).
- `repack_weight` accepts non-contiguous zero points (vllm-project/humming#204).
- The JIT cache key hashing works on FIPS-enabled systems (vllm-project/humming#187), and `nvrtc_compile` finds `libnvrtc-builtins` on Linux (vllm-project/humming#202).

**Performance**

- SM103 MXFP4 x MXFP8 MoE pipelines and heuristics (vllm-project/humming#206).
- SM90: padded K blocks and slabs are skipped (vllm-project/humming#183), and short-K indexed A8 MoE uses the warp-specialized ring (vllm-project/humming#208).
- Input quantization uses wider vectors on large SM90/SM100 grids (vllm-project/humming#197, vllm-project/humming#199).
- Faster JIT: NVRTC uses nvcc's CCCL unroll limit (vllm-project/humming#192), and helper builds are skipped when precompiled artifacts exist (vllm-project/humming#184).

**Packaging**

- On Linux, the `cu12` / `cu13` extras resolve nvcc, CCCL, the runtime headers and NVRTC through `cuda-toolkit`, so they match the toolkit version PyTorch pins (vllm-project/humming#211). Fixes #67595; alternative to #67596.

**New**

- Packed weight type conversion (vllm-project/humming#207). vLLM does not use it yet.

## Validation

GPU evaluation is incomplete: only one config has run, once per version. The other checks below are resolver runs and CPU-only compiles.

**GSM8K A/B** (B300, 1 GPU, 1319 questions, 5-shot, clean venv from `requirements/cuda.txt`; 0.1.19 swapped in via `PYTHONPATH`, separate `HUMMING_CACHE_DIR` per version):

| Config | 0.1.19 | 0.1.20 | CI threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nm-testing/Qwen3-30B-A3B-MXFP4A16`, `--quantization humming --linear-backend humming`, `VLLM_HUMMING_MOE_GEMM_TYPE=grouped_contiguous` | 89.46% (1550 tok/s) | 88.70% (1601 tok/s) | 86% |

The 0.76-point difference is 10 questions, about one standard error for a single run of this size, so one run per version cannot separate it from noise. Repeat runs and the small linear configs (`Qwen3-0.6B-MXFP8`, `Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct-FP8W8` with FP8 activations) have not run yet: the shared GPU queue did not reach them. The `lm-eval-humming` CI jobs cover those configs.

- **Clean venv** (`uv pip install -r requirements/cuda.txt`, then `VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 uv pip install -e .`): `uv pip check` passes, and every `humming` import statement in `vllm/` resolves against 0.1.20.
- **Kernel compiles:** six cached Humming kernels (sm_103a) compile through both the NVRTC and nvcc paths using only the pip toolchain from that venv.
- **Resolved toolchain** from `requirements/cuda.txt` (`uv pip install --dry-run`, Python 3.12, Linux):

| Install flow | nvcc / CCCL with 0.1.19 | nvcc / CCCL with 0.1.20 | Runtime headers |
|---|---|---|---|
| PyPI torch 2.14.0 (x86_64, aarch64) | 13.5.37 / 13.3.5.0.6 | 13.0.88 / 13.0.85 | 13.0.96 |
| torch `+cu132` | 13.5.37 / 13.3.5.0.6 | 13.2.78 / 13.2.75 | 13.2.75 |
| Rubin, torch 2.16 nightly `+cu134` | 13.5.37 / 13.3.5.0.6 | 13.4.59 / 13.3.4.2.1 | 13.4.49 |
| CUDA 12.6, `[cu12]` | 12.9.86 / 12.9.27 | 12.6.85 / 12.6.77 | 12.6.77 |

## Details

Two behavior changes come with the packaging fix:

- The pip-installed nvcc now follows PyTorch's toolkit version (13.0 on PyPI torch) instead of floating to the newest release. Humming's default compiler is NVRTC, which PyTorch already pinned, and Humming still prefers a newer system toolkit when present, so default code generation does not change.
- A `[cu12]` install against a CUDA 13 PyTorch now fails to resolve instead of installing a mixed environment. `CUDA_VERSION=12.9` Docker builds hit this, because there is no `torch==2.14.0+cu129` and the resolver falls back to the PyPI CUDA 13 wheel.

<details>
<summary>Background on #67595</summary>

`humming-kernels[cu13]` 0.1.19 required `nvidia-cuda-nvcc` and `nvidia-cuda-cccl` with no version, so they resolved to 13.5.37 / 13.3.5 while PyTorch pins the runtime headers and NVRTC through `cuda-toolkit==13.0.3`. CCCL requires the compiler minor version to equal the header minor version, so JIT builds that use the pip compiler with CCCL failed with `#error "CUDA compiler and CUDA toolkit headers are incompatible"`. With 0.1.19, Humming's main GEMM kernel failed this way on the nvcc path, as did FlashInfer's `sampling` module when `CUDA_HOME` pointed at the pip toolchain (measured on a clean `vllm==0.33.0` install); both compile with 0.1.20.

#67596 pins the toolchain to 13.0 in `requirements/cuda.txt` instead. It cannot install as written (`nvidia-cuda-nvvm` is not a PyPI package; the name is `nvidia-nvvm`), and a hard 13.0 pin would recreate the mismatch for cu132 and Rubin installs.

`site-packages/nvidia/cu13` is still not a complete `CUDA_HOME` for FlashInfer: it has no unversioned `libcudart.so`, so the link step needs one on the link path. This PR does not change that.

</details>

commits.pr_title: [Kernel] Bump DeepGEMM for SM90 paged-MQA metadata and mHC prenorm fixes
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Bump the DeepGEMM pin from `196f338` to `e84cd4f`, which adds exactly two fork commits: vllm-project/DeepGEMM#63 (SM90 paged-MQA metadata kernel compiled once for every batch size) and vllm-project/DeepGEMM#64 (SM90 mHC prenorm GEMM register-reuse fix, cherry-pick of deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM#448). Part of #64824.

## Claims

- On SM90 the DSA indexer's decode schedule-metadata kernel no longer JIT-compiles once per 32-row decode bucket; one compile serves every batch size. This removes the request-path compiles after `/health` that #67749 works around by warming every bucket at startup, so that warmup is not needed with this pin.
- The SM90 `tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm` kernel waits for its asynchronous WGMMA before reusing the register A operands. This is the fix #59129 patches into the header at build time; with it in the pin, that build-time patching is not needed.
- No vLLM code changes; the DeepGEMM Python API is unchanged.

## Validation

Not a duplicate: the only other open pin bump, #59503, targets `550036a`, which is already an ancestor of the current pin.

### End-to-end cold start

DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 + DSpark (k=5), TP4 on 4x H200, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.0+cu130. One run per arm, same host and GPUs, run back to back, every JIT cache (DeepGEMM, Triton, TileLang, FlashInfer, inductor, vLLM) empty at start. Both arms are this PR's commit installed against the `8070069e8` main wheel:

- **main**: the wheel's vendored DeepGEMM (pin `196f338`).
- **this PR**: the fork built at `e84cd4f` and picked up as the external `deep_gemm` package (`PYTHONPATH`), which `vllm.utils.deep_gemm` prefers over the vendored copy. This is DeepGEMM's own build of the pinned commit, not a wheel produced by vLLM's CMake.

After `/health`, `vllm bench serve` is run twice (cold pass, then steady pass). DeepGEMM compiles are counted by diffing `DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR` at `/health` and after each pass.

| arm | time-to-ready | metadata kernels at `/health` | DeepGEMM compiles after `/health` (cold / steady) | cold TTFT p99 | cold ITL p99 | cold out tok/s | steady TTFT p99 | steady out tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 936 s | 18 | 19 / 0 | 22.4 s | 1326 ms | 1220 | 1.96 s | 1405 |
| **this PR** | 901 s | 1 | 0 / 0 | 8.0 s | 449 ms | 1339 | 1.92 s | 1383 |

All 19 runtime compiles on main are `sm90_paged_mqa_logits_metadata` (37 metadata kernels in the cache by the end, versus 1 with this PR). All 4000 requests completed with 0 failures; DSpark was active in both arms (mean acceptance length 1.37 / 1.29 on random-token prompts). An earlier startup-only run of the same two arms gave 927 s / 917 s time-to-ready and the same 18 / 1 metadata kernels at `/health`.

<details><summary>Commands</summary>

```bash
# per arm: C=<empty dir>; the PR arm additionally sets PYTHONPATH=<DeepGEMM fork checkout built at e84cd4f>
DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR=$C/dg TRITON_CACHE_DIR=$C/triton TILELANG_CACHE_DIR=$C/tilelang \
FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BASE=$C/flashinfer VLLM_CACHE_ROOT=$C/vllm TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=$C/inductor \
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 --tensor-parallel-size 4 --trust-remote-code \
  --max-model-len 20480 --served-model-name m \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5}'

# after /health, twice (cold, steady):
vllm bench serve --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 --served-model-name m --trust-remote-code \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 256 --ignore-eos \
  --num-prompts 1000 --max-concurrency 192 --num-warmups 0 --seed 0 \
  --percentile-metrics ttft,tpot,itl,e2el --metric-percentiles 50,99
```

</details>

**Not done:** a wheel built by vLLM's CMake on the new pin (left to CI), repeated runs (one per arm, so the latency and throughput columns carry no variability estimate), an accuracy eval, and anything on H100/H20.

### DeepGEMM-level

H200, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.0+cu130.

Fork at the pinned commit `e84cd4f`, full extension build:

```bash
cd DeepGEMM/tests
python test_attention.py        # rc=0
python test_hyperconnection.py  # rc=0
```

- `test_attention.py`: 360 paged MQA logits cases (PAGE_KV 32/64, `next_n` 1/2/4, context up to 65536) and the zero-context test pass. The JIT cache holds 4 `sm90_paged_mqa_logits_metadata` kernels afterwards.
- `test_hyperconnection.py`: all 48 cases pass (24 original shapes, 24 configurations of the new split-K reference and repeatability test).

Metadata kernel, before vs after (from vllm-project/DeepGEMM#63):

- `get_paged_mqa_logits_metadata` output is bit-identical to the pre-change build on 216 tensors: batch 1-6144, `next_n` 1/2/4, ragged lengths, ~1M-token contexts with empty rows, one long row among short ones, PDL off and on. In every case a side-stream launch equals the default-stream result, and a CUDA graph captured with one set of context lengths and replayed after overwriting them equals an eager call on the new contents.
- That sweep compiles 24 metadata kernels before and 4 after.
- Launch time is unchanged (batch 512: 11.4 us → 11.3 us; batch 6144: 20.4 us → 20.1 us).

## Details

**Metadata kernel.** `sm90_paged_mqa_logits_metadata` was templated on the batch size rounded up to 32. The value is only a loop bound and a shared-memory offset, so it is now a launch argument. #67749 measured the effect of the missing compiles on DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark (k=5) on H100 TP8: 28 runtime compiles after `/health` and a cold-start TTFT p99 of 24.8 s.

**mHC prenorm tradeoff.** The fix removes the overlap between a stage's WGMMA and the next stage's A-operand load, so the kernel is slower when it runs without split-K. On H200 that is about 10% in most shapes (e.g. m=4096, k=28672: 109 us → 122 us, single runs); split-K shapes are mixed. The upstream author reports up to +39% at large M on H20. In vLLM `compute_num_split` only reaches one split above roughly 4,200 tokens per batch on H200 (132 SMs), so this lands on large prefill batches rather than decode. I could not reproduce the race itself on H200: the regression test also passes with the original header. deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM#449 reports it on H20 and discusses a double-buffered follow-up that recovers the cost; that is not included here.

commits.pr_title: [Perf][MoE] Add NVIDIA L4 FP8 fused MoE config for Qwen3-30B-A3B
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

There is no fused MoE config for the NVIDIA L4 (AWS g6) in `vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/configs/`. So Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 at TP2 on L4 runs on the default heuristic and logs `Using default MoE config. Performance might be sub-optimal!`. This PR adds a tuned L4 config for that shape:

- `E=128,N=384,device_name=NVIDIA_L4,dtype=fp8_w8a8,block_shape=[128,128].json`

Other Qwen3-30B-A3B FP8 checkpoints with the same expert shape load the same file, for example Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-FP8. I only measured Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8.

## Claims

- **Kernel.** Fused MoE kernel time is 1.2-5.4% lower for 7-240 and 385-528 tokens in every run, and 0.6-1.6% lower for 4 and 6 tokens. 5 tokens is equal.
- **Main's config elsewhere.** All other batch sizes (1-3, 241-384 and 529 and up) use exactly main's config. I checked this by computing the lookup for every batch size up to 16384.
- **Serving, concurrency 8.** Throughput is +2.2% and median TPOT is -4.0% (medians of 3 runs; Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8, TP2, 2x L4).
- **Serving, concurrency 32.** No measurable change.
- **Serving, concurrency 1.** This runs main's config (1-token decode, 1024-token prefill), so it only shows the noise floor.
- **Accuracy.** GSM8K is unchanged.

## Validation

Setup:
- NVIDIA L4 24 GB, driver 580.159.04: AWS g6.12xlarge for tuning and serving, g6.xlarge for the kernel A/B.
- torch 2.14.0+cu132, Triton 3.8.0.
- vLLM main at feed3a4475. The MoE config lookup, `get_default_config` and the FP8 Triton MoE path are unchanged between that commit and this branch.

Tuning (default search space and batch sizes):

```bash
python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_moe.py --model Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 --tp-size 2 --dtype fp8_w8a8 --tune
```

**Kernel.**
- `benchmark_moe.py` without `--tune` on 1x L4: once without the file, and once with `VLLM_TUNED_CONFIG_FOLDER` pointing at it.
- 4 runs per arm in ABBA order (main, PR, PR, main, main, PR, PR, main).
- The batch sizes cover both edges of every range where this file's config differs from main's, and the points where main's default changes (5, 9, 17, 65). They also include spot checks where the config is main's.
- The command and raw output are in the comments.

**Serving.**
- Each run used a fresh `vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 -tp 2 --seed 0`, with 3 runs per arm, alternating between arms.
- The server log confirmed which config each arm loaded: `Using configuration from ...NVIDIA_L4...` versus `Using default MoE config`.
- The serving runs and GSM8K used the first commit's file. The second commit only changes 241-384, 529-768 and 1281-1792 tokens to main's config. Decode at concurrency 1, 8 and 32, and the 1024-token prefill chunks, use the same entries in both versions.

```bash
vllm bench serve --model Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 256 --random-range-ratio 0.0 \
  --num-prompts {30,100,200} --max-concurrency {1,8,32} --ignore-eos --seed 42 --num-warmups 4
```

The raw `vllm bench serve` output of every run is in the comments, with the GSM8K output.

**Accuracy.** `python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --port 8000` (5-shot, 1319 questions, temperature 0): default 0.889, this PR 0.893.

## Details

The lookup picks the nearest key (ties go to the lower key), so each entry serves a range of batch sizes:

- **Tuned:** 4-240 tokens (keys 4 to 128, and 224) and 385-528 tokens (key 512).
- **Main's default config:** 1-3 tokens (keys 1, 2), 241-384 tokens (key 256), and 529 tokens and up (keys 544, 768, 1024, 1536, 2048, 3072, 4096).

- **Why the default above 240 and 528 tokens.** The tuned configs there use `BLOCK_SIZE_M` 16 (up to 256) and 32 (512). They lose once the average tokens per expert passes the M tile: up to 6% slower at 320 tokens, up to 14% at 384, and 2-5% at 640. So keys holding the default end each tuned range where it is still faster in every run.
- **The 224 key.** It holds the config the tuner chose for 64, 96, 128 and 256. This lets the 256 key hold the default.
- **1 and 2 tokens.** The tuned configs were faster in `benchmark_moe.py` but not end to end: decode at concurrency 1 was about 0.7% slower with them. The benchmark replays the same inputs, and the active experts' weights (at most 16 experts, about 38 MB) fit in the L4's 48 MB L2. So the default is kept.
- **1536-4096.** The tuned configs were not measurably faster, so the default is kept.

commits.pr_title: [Doc] Routed experts: row storage, replica affinity, sizing and cache resets
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Bring `docs/training/routed_experts.md` in line with what `main` does today, for RL users running routed experts return without the session object store:

- **Row storage**: rows live in the host memory of each engine's first TP worker, keyed by KV block hash, and last as long as their KV.
- **Replica affinity**: later turns hit only on the engine holding the prefix; route sessions with consistent hashing and use `routed_experts_prompt_start`.
- **Sizing `max_bytes`**: a smaller value does not save memory; size the KV cache for the sessions instead.
- **Requirements**: drop the KV connector rejection list, which `main` does not enforce; explain what a prefill/decode deployment actually does.
- **Weight updates and cache resets**: any prefix-cache reset drops all rows; `reset_connector` decides whether the KV connector tier survives, and how to keep reusing it via `routed_experts_prompt_start`.

## Test Plan

Docs only. Every statement was checked against `main` (`vllm/config/vllm.py::_verify_aux_output_compatibility`, `Scheduler.reset_prefix_cache`, `AuxOutputConnector.cap_external_hit`, `EngineCore.sleep` / `pause_scheduler`). 
## Test Result

A fresh low-effort reader agent answered six scenario questions (prefill/decode deployment, sleep with and without `reset_connector`, pause without clearing the cache, `reset_prefix_cache`) from the page alone; all answers were correct after two wording fixes.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Kimi-K3] Capture all mixed CUDA graphs with RecoverSSM
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Remove the RecoverSSM-only cap on mixed PIECEWISE CUDA graph sizes. With `--use-replayssm` on Kimi-K3/K3.1 (KDA) and speculative decoding, the cap dropped every mixed graph above `max_num_seqs * (1 + num_speculative_tokens)` tokens, so steps of that size ran eagerly. The guard came from #55774.

## Claims

- Mixed PIECEWISE graphs are captured for all configured sizes again when RecoverSSM is on. With `max_num_seqs=128` and 4 speculative tokens, 83 graphs are captured instead of 59, and the 24 graphs for 641-1024 tokens no longer run eagerly.
- Fixes a ShareGPT QPS 8 low-latency regression on Kimi K3.1 Pro (TPOT 53.3 ms with 59 graphs, 31-36 ms with all 83).

## Validation

Unit test, CPU only (`tests/v1/cudagraph/test_cudagraph_manager.py`):

```
pytest tests/v1/cudagraph/test_cudagraph_manager.py::test_recoverssm_keeps_mixed_graphs_past_the_decode_token_cap
```

- On main: `assert 4 > (2 * 3)` fails, with mixed sizes `[1, 2, 4]`.
- With this change: passes.

End to end (internal GB300 runs of Kimi K3.1 Pro, TP8 + DCP8, DSpark k=4, `--use-replayssm`, `max_num_seqs=128`, ShareGPT QPS 8):

- NVIDIA K3.1 branch build dbbc9e3 with the guard, 59 of 83 mixed graphs captured: TPOT 53.3 ms, TTFT 2989 ms, 1378 tok/s.
- Same build with only `max_num_seqs` raised to 208, which keeps all 83 graphs under the guard: TPOT 31.4 ms, TTFT 318 ms, 1523 tok/s.
- Nightly 615c9d64 (guard present) with this change applied at runtime: 83 of 83 PIECEWISE graphs captured, QPS 8 TPOT 36.18 ms.

## Details

Removing the cap is safe because:

- RecoverSSM's verify capacity is per request (`num_spec + 1` tokens), not per step.
- `KimiK3KDAMetadataBuilder` routes rows wider than `num_spec + 1` to the non-spec path (`vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/kda_metadata.py`, with a comment naming these capture dummies), so they never reach the RecoverSSM verify path or its capacity check.
- KDA `_forward` is an eager break at replay, so no graph holds RecoverSSM shapes.
- The cost is about 0.57 GiB per rank of extra graph pool.

No open PR covers this. #67590, #58863 and #61309 add a GDN RecoverSSM flag to the same condition. If their GDN metadata builder does not route wide rows to the non-spec path, they will need to keep the cap for GDN.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Report reasoning_tokens in /inference/v1/generate derender usage
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

`/inference/v1/generate` with `output_mode: "derender"` now reports `usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens` in batch and stream mode, summed over the choices, as `/v1/chat/completions` does. Fixes #65360.

**Stacked on #64041.** The first commit (b5701018c5) is #64041 cherry-picked onto main; review only the commits after it (170677d681, 658be9d6a6). This PR reuses the reasoning-token count #64041 adds to `OnlineDerenderer._parse_and_assemble`, so it can't land first. I'll rebase once #64041 merges.

## Claims

- With `--reasoning-parser`, batch and stream generate derender usage include `completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`. Before this change it was `null` on both paths.
- The count matches `/v1/chat/completions`, including with `include_reasoning: false` and summed across choices when `n > 1`. Stream with `n > 1` works here, unlike chat derender in #64041, because generate keeps a live parser per choice.
- Without a reasoning parser (or with only a tool parser), `completion_tokens_details` stays `null`, as on chat.
- `tokens` and `text` output modes are unchanged.

## Validation

**New end-to-end test (1x L4):** `test_derender_mode_usage_reports_reasoning_tokens` in `test_serving_tokens.py`. It starts a real server with Qwen3-0.6B and `--reasoning-parser deepseek_v3`, reusing the server fixture of the existing reasoning tests. It compares generate derender usage with `/v1/chat/completions` for batch with `include_reasoning: true` and for stream with `include_reasoning: false`. Both use `n=2` with seeded sampling (greedy rejects `n > 1`).

```bash
pytest tests/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/test_serving_tokens.py -k test_derender_mode_usage_reports_reasoning_tokens
```

Before (b5701018c5, #64041 only, with the new test file):

```text
E       AssertionError: assert None == {'reasoning_tokens': 62}
E       KeyError: 'completion_tokens_details'
2 failed, 26 deselected in 49.40s
```

After (this branch):

```text
2 passed, 26 deselected in 49.40s
```

Usage from the issue's repro request on the same server, run twice per mode; chat and generate matched on every run:

```text
batch,  include_reasoning=true:  chat and generate {'prompt_tokens': 16, 'completion_tokens': 64, 'completion_tokens_details': {'reasoning_tokens': 62}}
stream, include_reasoning=false: chat and generate {'prompt_tokens': 16, 'completion_tokens': 64, 'completion_tokens_details': {'reasoning_tokens': 62}}
```

**CPU unit tests (macOS):** both affected unit-test files pass.

```bash
pytest tests/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/test_generate_stream.py \
       tests/entrypoints/scale_out/derender/test_derender_stream.py
```

```text
183 passed, 1 xfailed in 213.75s
```

`pre-commit run` passes on the changed files. These tests run in CI in the `entrypoints-integration-api-server` step (`pytest entrypoints/scale_out`).

## Details

**Root cause:** `ServingTokens` built `UsageInfo` from token counts only, in `_build_response_fields` (batch) and in the final stream usage chunk. #63103 left `reasoning_tokens` out of scope.

**What changed:**
- **Batch:** `OnlineDerenderer.derender_text_choices` now also returns `completion_tokens_details`. It sums the per-choice count from `_parse_and_assemble` (#64041). It is `None` unless `--reasoning-parser` is set.
- **Stream:** `serve_tokens_stream_generator` keeps each choice's output token IDs. At the end, `OnlineDerenderer.stream_completion_tokens_details` counts them with that choice's `ChatStreamProcessor` parser. Coupled chat does the same.

**Limitation:** per-chunk `continuous_usage_stats` usage still has no details. Coupled chat recounts every token on every chunk to fill them; I left that out to keep this small. It's noted in the docs.

**Not a duplicate:** no open PR references #65360 or touches generate usage. #64041 covers `/v1/chat/completions/derender` only and lists generate as out of scope. #64935 covers `/v1/chat/completions/batch` only.

commits.pr_title: [Kimi K3][Specialized decode] Run causal DSpark draft blocks on CAKE (TP / DEP)
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Kimi K3.1 specialized decode: causal DSpark draft blocks (TP / DEP) whose `k × heads` exceeds 64 now run on CAKE as one `[R, k, H]` decode row per request under the kernel's causal mask. CAKE launches are length-balanced. Ported from wzhao18's branch, scoped to the TP / DEP path on top of `main`.

## Claims

- **DEP (96 draft heads, k = 4)**: causal draft attention costs 0.27–0.89× of `main` at every batch size measured (1–128 requests per rank), at 100K contexts and with serving-like mixed contexts.
- **TP4 (24 heads)**: 0.39–1.03× with mixed contexts. With uniform 100K contexts it is 0.74–1.14×: up to 14% slower at 16–24 requests (see Details).
- **TP8 (12 heads)**: unchanged. `k × heads = 48` keeps `causal_folded_decode`.
- **Non-causal CAKE fold** (Kimi K3 DSpark, 64 heads) is also length-balanced. It removes CAKE's unsplit-long-request cliffs, e.g. 2,753 → 1,065 µs at 32 mixed-context requests (64 heads), and 2.2–2.7× at 64–128 requests (8 heads). Elsewhere it is within measurement noise.
- **Unchanged**: the DCP draft path (`DraftDcp`), the CAKE workspace cap and its trtllm-gen fallback, and `draft_forward_mqa` returning `None` for batches it cannot fold.

## Validation

**Tests**: `pytest tests/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_specialized_decode_draft_attention.py` on GB300: 50 passed (35 on `main`).

**Kernel benchmark**:
- Setup:
  - one GB300, one draft layer, CUDA-graph replay, median of 5 × 30 replays;
  - k = 4, plan length 1M (as captured), FP8 query and KV, page 64.
- Columns:
  - `main`: `causal_folded_decode`;
  - this PR: `folded_decode(causal=True)`.
- Contexts:
  - "100K": every request at 100K;
  - "mixed": 40K–250K plus one 600K request.

Causal draft, µs per layer (this PR / `main`):

| requests / rank | DEP 96h, 100K | DEP 96h, mixed | TP4 24h, 100K | TP4 24h, mixed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 36.7 / 55.8 | 166 / 262 | 22.6 / 30.6 | 82.7 / 96.4 |
| 8 | 264 / 310 | 389 / 1,425 | 100 / 98.4 | 191 / 343 |
| 16 | 492 / 643 | 774 / 1,060 | 201 / 186 | 290 / 735 |
| 24 | 718 / 1,143 | 1,269 / 1,549 | 308 / 270 | 437 / 998 |
| 32 | 1,004 / 1,289 | 1,541 / 2,182 | 352 / 362 | 562 / 1,445 |
| 64 | 2,003 / 2,572 | 2,874 / 3,583 | 722 / 735 | 1,037 / 1,007 |
| 128 | 3,997 / 4,980 | 5,794 / 7,508 | 1,493 / 1,484 | 2,067 / 2,493 |

Accuracy, vs an FP32 causal reference (6 requests, 2K–9K contexts), max error relative to the reference's max magnitude:

| heads | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 96 | 1.8% | 1.8% |
| 24 | 2.0% | 2.1% |

**Noise**: with identical code on both sides, the ratio still moves within 0.86–1.07. Differences under ~7% are not significant.

**Not covered**:
- End-to-end serving.
- Draft acceptance rate.
- DCP: this PR does not change it.

## Details

**Why CAKE for wide causal blocks.**
- `causal_folded_decode` runs the shared context through the cute-dsl LSE decode, which tiles at most 128 query heads per row. At 96 heads it cannot fold even two tokens, so each draft token streams the whole context.
- CAKE takes the `[R, k, H]` block as one row with a causal mask. Each KV tile is read once per 128 `(token, head)` rows: 3 times per request at 96 × 4, instead of 4.
- At `k × heads ≤ 64` the cute-dsl fold already reads the context once per request and splits long contexts better. On a TP8 mixed batch at 44–96 requests, CAKE was up to 1.6× slower there, so those blocks keep `causal_folded_decode`.

**`cake_balance`.**
- CAKE plans its KV split from the batch shape alone. Over bands of batch sizes it leaves the longest request unsplit, and that one request then holds the whole launch.
- When CAKE's plan splits the longest request at most 2 ways within 4 waves, the balanced launches (the existing DCP split tiers, now also on CAKE) move long requests to their own CAKE launches.
- The decision is made on the GPU from the actual lengths, so it is CUDA-graph safe.
- The load-time reservation also sizes the balanced launches' workspace.

**Tradeoffs and limitations.**
- **TP4 uniform 100K, 16–24 requests**: 8–14% slower than `main`. With mixed contexts at the same sizes it is 2–2.5× faster, so CAKE is kept for `k × heads > 64`.
- **Pre-existing, not fixed here**: a non-causal CAKE fold of exactly 64 rows (e.g. 16 heads × k = 4) is rejected by FlashInfer ("generic tail supports max_seq_len <= 4096") at plan lengths above 4K. The current fallback re-raises it, on `main` as with this PR.

**Taken from the original branch, and not.**
- Taken: the causal CAKE row, `cake_balance` and its workspace, and `balanced_decode` on CAKE.
- Not taken:
  - The DCP routing change and the causal cute-dsl (LSE) fold it uses.
  - The removal of the CAKE workspace cap and fallback. An eager batch planned at a shorter length can need more workspace than the load-time reservation, and a 256 × k5 DEP batch would reserve 4.9 GiB.
  - Raising instead of returning `None` from `draft_forward_mqa`.

**Not duplicated**: no open PR changes `drafter/attention.py`'s causal path. The original branch was a PR against the `k31` branch on a fork, written before `causal_folded_decode` landed on `main`.

commits.pr_title: [KV Offload] Leave CPU KV offload buffers out of core dumps
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Leave the CPU KV offload buffers out of core dumps with `madvise(MADV_DONTDUMP)`. A crashing worker no longer writes its whole CPU KV cache, often 100+ GiB per rank, into its core file.

## Claims

- Core dumps of a worker using `SimpleCPUOffloadConnector` or `OffloadingConnector` shrink by the size of the CPU KV cache. The rest of the process is still dumped.
- Covers `alloc_host_buffer` (`SimpleCPUOffloadConnector`), `SharedOffloadRegion` (`OffloadingConnector` CPU tier on CUDA and XPU, every tiering setup, HiSparse's shared host region; segmented regions included) and the KVCR local DRAM tier.
- No behavior change otherwise: one `madvise` call per buffer at startup, through a new `exclude_from_core_dump` helper in `vllm/utils/host_memory.py`. Where `mmap.MADV_DONTDUMP` is missing it does nothing, and if the call fails it only logs a warning.

## Validation

GB300, Linux 7.0 arm64, default `coredump_filter` (0x33), `ulimit -c unlimited`, `core_pattern` writing a file. main is a4910b4128.

**Unit tests.** The new tests check, through `/proc/self/smaps`, that every page of the buffer has the `dd` (VM_DONTDUMP) flag. They fail on main and pass on this branch:

```
pytest -q tests/v1/simple_kv_offload/test_host_buffer.py tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_shared_offload_region.py -k core_dumps
```

<details>
<summary>Output</summary>

```

E   assert 327680 == 0
     +  where 327680 = core_dumped_bytes(264350720983040, (264350720983040 + 327680))
     +    where 327680 = <vllm.v1.kv_offload.cpu.shared_offload_region.SharedOffloadRegion object at 0xf06cf33d2150>.total_size_bytes
FAILED tests/v1/simple_kv_offload/test_host_buffer.py::test_buffer_is_left_out_of_core_dumps[False]
FAILED tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_shared_offload_region.py::test_region_is_left_out_of_core_dumps[1]
FAILED tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_shared_offload_region.py::test_region_is_left_out_of_core_dumps[3]
3 failed, 1 skipped, 81 deselected in 6.97s

# this PR
SKIPPED [1] tests/v1/simple_kv_offload/conftest.py:28: needs 1 free hugepages of some size
3 passed, 1 skipped, 81 deselected in 12.18s
```

</details>

`pytest -q tests/v1/simple_kv_offload tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering`: 1146 passed, 19 skipped, 2 failed, 104 errors. The failures (two `test_p2p_lifecycle_e2e.py` tests) and errors (teardown of `TestTieringOffloadingManager` failure-path tests) are identical on main in this environment: `tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering` gives 720 passed, 2 failed, 104 errors on both.

**Real core dumps.** I sent `SIGABRT` to a process holding an offload buffer and measured the core file the kernel wrote:

- a Python process mapping a 2 GiB buffer with `alloc_host_buffer` or `SharedOffloadRegion` (files unlinked after the barrier, as in serving), then `os.abort()`;
- the EngineCore process of `vllm serve`, after one completion request:

```
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct --gpu-memory-utilization 0.3 --max-model-len 4096 --enforce-eager \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"SimpleCPUOffloadConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"cpu_bytes_to_use":8589934592}}'
# and with '{"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"cpu_bytes_to_use":2000000000}}'
kill -ABRT <EngineCore pid>
```

| Process | CPU KV cache | Core file, main | Core file, this PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Python, `alloc_host_buffer` | 2 GiB | 3.30 GiB | 1.29 GiB |
| Python, `SharedOffloadRegion` | 2 GiB | 3.29 GiB | 1.29 GiB |
| EngineCore, `SimpleCPUOffloadConnector` | 8 GiB | 12.72 GiB | 4.70 GiB |
| EngineCore, `OffloadingConnector` | 1.86 GiB | 6.56 GiB | 4.69 GiB |

Each core file shrinks by the size of the CPU KV cache. In `/proc/<EngineCore pid>/smaps`, the VM_DONTDUMP mappings total 0.07 GiB on main and 1.93 GiB with this PR for `OffloadingConnector`, and 8.07 GiB with this PR for `SimpleCPUOffloadConnector`. These dumps ran on the PR's first revision; later revisions only moved the helper and covered the KVCR tier.

## Details

- **Root cause.** The kernel dumps private anonymous memory and, by default, anonymous shared memory (`coredump_filter` bits 0 and 1). `alloc_host_buffer` is a private anonymous mapping. `SharedOffloadRegion` maps tmpfs files that are unlinked once every worker has mapped them; the kernel then treats them as anonymous shared memory and dumps them too. So the whole CPU KV cache ends up in every worker's core file. On a node with eight ranks and 100+ GiB each, that is close to a terabyte written on a crash, which can fill the node or container disk.
- **Why `MADV_DONTDUMP`.** It works per address range and takes precedence over `coredump_filter`, so only the KV cache is skipped. `ulimit -c 0` or `PR_SET_DUMPABLE` would drop the whole dump. `SharedOffloadRegion` is marked after its segment files are mapped with `MAP_FIXED`, because each new mapping replaces the old one's flags. Each process marks its own mapping.
- **Opt-out.** There is none: KV cache contents do not help debug a crash, and keeping them out also keeps request data out of core files. A flag can be added if someone needs them.
- **Not covered.** Buffers allocated as pinned torch tensors rather than mappings: the single-tier `OffloadingConnector` CPU tier on platforms other than CUDA and XPU, and HiSparse's non-shared host pool. Their addresses are not page-aligned mappings that vLLM owns, so they would need a different approach.
- **Not exercised here.** HugeTLB buffers (no free huge pages on the test machine; the kernel accepts `MADV_DONTDUMP` on HugeTLB mappings) and the KVCR tier (needs the `kvcr` package). The real dumps used TP=1.
- **No `vllm_runner` test.** Dump size is not an API result. The unit tests check the functions that allocate the buffers, and the dumps above check a served model.
- Test runs used a libc polyfill for `os.memfd_create`, which the uv-managed CPython used here lacks.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Bound CoW block-copy transient to avoid OOM near the memory limit
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

> **Note:** @zjy0516 wrote this description and the current approach (commits from `21e3b27` onward, pushed as maintainer edits). The PR's original revision, by the PR author, bounded the gather to 256 MiB chunks; see "Previous revisions" below.

## Overview

`copy_kv_cache_blocks_inplace` (`vllm/v1/worker/utils.py`) ran `blocks[dst] = blocks[src]`, which gathers every source block into one device temporary before scattering it. KV cache blocks can be tens of MiB (Mamba state, or blocks spanning all layers), so a wave of copy-on-write copies for partial prefix-cache hits asks for GiBs that a deployment near `gpu_memory_utilization` does not have, and OOMs. On GPU, this PR copies the blocks with one Triton kernel that moves each contiguous byte run straight from source to destination, with no temporary.

## Claims

- GPU block copies no longer allocate block-sized temporaries; only the descriptor table (24 bytes per run) goes to the device.
- The copy runs 21-28x faster on the GPU than the indexed copy (about 3.2 TB/s vs 117 GiB/s), and host submission stays about 1 ms with thousands of runs.
- Qwen3.5-35B-A3B under async scheduling: copy-on-write waves finish 17% faster than `main` (median 1148 ms vs 1383 ms).
- No change for CPU caches or chained copies (a block that is both a source and a destination): they keep the indexed copy.

## Validation

**Tests** (GB200, CUDA 13.0):

```bash
pytest tests/v1/worker/test_attn_utils.py tests/v1/worker/test_utils.py
# 134 passed
```

The existing block-copy tests (all `KVCacheLayout`s, separate head groups, virtual block splitting, overlaid Mamba/attention views) now also run on CUDA, which takes the kernel path. `test_copy_kv_cache_blocks_inplace_cuda_skips_gather_temporary` fails on `main` and passes here:

```
# main
E       AssertionError: assert (20972032 - 16777216) < 1048576
# this PR
passed
```

`test_copy_kv_cache_blocks_inplace_cuda_unaligned_blocks` covers runs that are not 8-byte aligned.

**GPU time of one copy call** (GB200; the stream is kept busy so host submission is hidden, as under async scheduling):

| Copies | indexed (`main`) | `cuMemcpyBatchAsync` | Triton (this PR) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 250 x 40 MiB, 1 view | 83.7 ms | 4.10 ms | 3.03 ms |
| 128 x 2 MiB, 10 views | 21.6 ms | 5.25 ms (host blocked 488 ms) | 0.79 ms |
| 1000 x 2 MiB, 10 views | 167.5 ms | 41.0 ms (host blocked 524 ms) | 6.04 ms |

`cuMemcpyBatchAsync` (copy engines) was the first alternative tried. On 2 MiB runs it only reaches about 476 GiB/s, and once about 1000 descriptors are queued behind busy work, the call blocks the host until the stream drains, which defeats async scheduling.

**E2E, async scheduling** (GB200 x1, `Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-FP8`, `--enable-prefix-caching --mamba-cache-mode align --prefix-match-unit 64 --async-scheduling`). Each wave warms a 2500-token prefix, then sends 256 requests sharing it with 100 new tokens each and 32 output tokens; up to 1020 copies land in one step. Median of 4 waves:

| | wave time | copy host time per call (max) |
|---|---:|---:|
| `main` | 1383 ms | 1.3 ms |
| `cuMemcpyBatchAsync` | 1197 ms | 57-67 ms |
| this PR | 1148 ms (1076-1235) | 1.4-1.8 ms |

**E2E accuracy** (GB200 x1, `ibm-granite/granite-4.0-h-tiny`, `--enable-prefix-caching --mamba-cache-mode align --prefix-match-unit 16`, GSM8K 20-shot, 1319 questions, concurrency 64). The 16-token match unit is finer than the 400-token block, so shared few-shot prefixes hit mid-block and take copy-on-write copies.

| | accuracy | prefix cache hit rate |
|---|---:|---:|
| `main` | 0.7885 | 87.9% |
| this PR | 0.7877 | 87.9% |

## Details

**Root cause.** The right-hand side of `blocks[dst] = blocks[src]` is a materializing gather of `len(src)` blocks. Profiling and warmup never run a copy-on-write, so no memory is reserved for it.

**Implementation.** Each cache view's copies are split into contiguous byte runs (trailing contiguous dims fold into one run), which covers padded, strided, overlaid and kernel-block-split views and the ReplaySSM trackers. All runs go to one Triton launch on the current stream, in the widest word that divides every address and size, so it stays ordered after block zeroing and before the forward pass, like the indexed copy it replaces. Kernel warmup compiles the kernel when prefix caching is enabled, so the first copy-on-write does not JIT mid-serving.

**Chained copies.** The kernel copies runs concurrently, so a block that is both a source and a destination falls back to the indexed copy, which reads all sources first. Copy-on-write destinations are freshly allocated blocks, so this does not happen in serving today.

**Limitations.** Overlaid views of one storage may write the same destination bytes twice with identical data; block-level disjointness assumes no two views of one storage are shifted against each other, which no allocator produces today. ROCm runs the same Triton kernel but was not tested locally (the AMD mirror of the V1 Worker CI step runs these tests). XPU and CPU keep the indexed copy.

**Previous revisions.** This PR first bounded the gather to 256 MiB chunks, which still needs unreserved memory and keeps the slow indexed copy, then tried `cuMemcpyBatchAsync`, replaced for the reasons above.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Only fuse RMSNorms that normalize over the last dim
commits.pr_body:
### Overview Split out of #60648 as @hmellor suggested. `RMSNormFuser` matched any `x * rsqrt(mean(x**2) + eps)`, whatever dim the mean was over, so norms that normalize over another dim (e.g. timm's `RmsNorm2d`, which means over the channels of NCHW) were fused into vLLM's last-dim `RMSNorm` and normalized over the wrong dim. ### Claims → `_variance_eps` only matches a mean over `-1`, as its docstring (`rsqrt(mean(x**2, -1) + eps)`) already says it should → Norms written with a positive last-dim index are left unfused too, which is perf only; ones whose class name ends in `RMSNorm` still get the existing "left unfused" warning ### Validation → Unit test: `pytest tests/models/transformers/fusers/test_rms_norm.py` 37 passed, including the new `ChannelRMSNorm` case in `test_non_rms_norms_are_not_matched` → The case it guards: Without the check the fuser matches the new test norm, timm's real `RmsNorm2d`, and both channel-mean variants (`weight.reshape(1, -1, 1, 1)` and `weight * x`); with it none of them match, and the last-dim `RMSNorm` still does → Where it showed up: Gemma 3n's MobileNetV5 vision tower (timm `RmsNorm2d`) on the Transformers backend in #60648 ### Details → Not a duplicate: No open PR touches `RMSNormFuser` or channel-mean norms; the only match for the searches is #60648, which this is split out of → AI assistance: AI assistance was used; I reviewed every line and ran the tests above

commits.pr_title: [Perf][KDA] Export Triton prefill checkpoints for Bailing V3
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Let the KDA layers of Bailing V3 (`BailingMoeV3ForCausalLM`, e.g. Ling-3.0-flash) export align-mode prefill checkpoints, using the per-sequence buffer path #67866 added for GLM-5.3-Flash and Kimi-K3: the Triton chunk recurrence writes each checkpoint's state into a `[N, H, V, K]` buffer, and `FlashKDAPrefillCheckpointExporter` moves it into the checkpoint block together with the conv window. With prefix caching on, a prompt is then no longer split at its last Mamba block boundary.

Follow-up to #67866. No open PR covers Bailing V3 or the shared FLA `chunk_kda` entry point.

## Claims

- The shared FLA `chunk_kda` (`vllm/third_party/flash_linear_attention/ops/kda.py`), which Bailing V3 calls, forwards `checkpoint_state` / `checkpoint_offsets` to `chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_h`. Before, its `**kwargs` would have silently dropped them.
- `BailingMoeV3KimiDeltaAttention` declares checkpoint alignment 64 and exports the checkpoint after its Triton prefill. It reserves the buffer only in `align` mode.
- GLM-5.3-Flash, Kimi-K3 and Bailing V3 now share two small helpers in `kda_checkpoint.py` that reserve and fetch the buffer. GLM and K3 behave as before.
- Ling-3.0-flash TP2 on GB300: TTFT -23% / -24% / -23% at concurrency 1 / 4 / 16; gsm8k with prefix-cache hits unchanged.
- Ling-3.0-flash TP2 on MI355X (same shared FLA path): TTFT -20% at concurrency 1.

## Validation

GB300:

```bash
pytest tests/models/kimi_k3/test_kda.py tests/models/glm5next/test_kda_recurrent.py \
  tests/kernels/mamba/test_checkpoint_exporter.py tests/kernels/fla
# 1930 passed, 7 skipped
```

- `test_triton_kda_checkpoint_correctness` now also runs the shared FLA `chunk_kda` (gate and beta precomputed, as Bailing V3 does). The checkpoints match a naive fp32 recurrence, and the output and final state match the run without checkpoints. Without the pass-through, the FLA cases fail.
- `test_prefill_checkpoint_resumes_suffix` (GLM layer forward, Triton) still passes with the helpers.

`inclusionAI/Ling-3.0-flash` (BF16), 2x GB300, TP2, `--enable-prefix-caching` (align mode, block size 1024), `--moe-backend triton` (see Details), 8192-token step budget. Baseline is main at `9e6c6b007a`; two fresh servers per arm, interleaved, mean of both.

| ISL 8000 / OSL 32, concurrency | TTFT ms, main → PR | total tok/s, main → PR | TPOT ms, main → PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 187.7 → 145.2 (-23%) | 25,520 → 29,474 | 4.08 → 4.09 |
| 4 | 408.4 → 309.8 (-24%) | 45,091 → 50,761 | 9.78 → 10.40 |
| 16 | 728.4 → 561.8 (-23%) | 61,567 → 64,344 | 43.7 → 46.2 |

Without a checkpoint, the scheduler ends an 8000-token prompt's first step at 7168 (7 × 1024) to save the state, and the prompt needs a second step. With a checkpoint, it runs in one step. There were no prefix-cache hits in either arm. The unsplit prefill delays other requests' decode steps, so TPOT rises 6% at concurrency 4 and 16.

| `tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --num-shots 20` (fixed few-shot prefix, 74% / 99% of prompt tokens hit in runs 1 / 2), 4 runs per arm | main | PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| accuracy | 0.8218 / 0.8241 / 0.8188 / 0.8234 | 0.8211 / 0.8317 / 0.8226 / 0.8324 |

Same model on ROCm: 2x MI355X, TP2, BF16, `--enable-prefix-caching` (align mode), ISL 8000 / OSL 32, concurrency 1, this branch against main `9e6c6b007a`. Two cold requests per arm after one warmup request (excluded):

| request | TTFT ms, main → PR | end-to-end latency ms, main → PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 247.16 → 197.15 (-20.2%) | 456.04 → 404.28 (-11.4%) |
| 2 | 245.20 → 196.68 (-19.8%) | 454.44 → 403.79 (-11.1%) |
| mean | 246.18 → 196.91 (-20.0%) | 455.24 → 404.03 (-11.2%) |

Concurrency 4 / 16 and gsm8k were not run on MI355X.

`VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error` server on this branch: checkpointed prefills and prefix-hit resumes from the stored checkpoints (2048 / 4096 / 7168 cached tokens), no sync errors.

## Details

- Q, K and V have separate inputs and conv states in Bailing V3, so the layer calls the exporter once per projection; only the Q call stores the recurrent state. This avoids concatenating QKV just for the export.
- Buffer: `max_num_seqs × local heads × 128 × 128` in the state dtype, reserved from the shared grow-only workspace (Ling-3.0-flash TP2: 16 heads, 1 MiB per sequence with an fp32 state).
- `--moe-backend triton` is only needed because Ling-3.0-flash does not start on GB300 with the default MoE backend: FlashInfer's TRT-LLM routing kernel allows at most 32 experts per group, and this model has 512 / 8 = 64. That is unrelated to this change.
- An unsplit prefill can delay other requests' decode steps in that step, as with FlashKDA.
- On ROCm, Bailing V3 runs the same shared FLA `chunk_kda` and layer code, so it gets checkpoints too (serving numbers above; the unit tests were run on GB300 only).
- AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for the implementation and the validation above.

commits.pr_title: [Docs] Add Ask AI widget
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Add an "Ask AI" assistant to the docs site, replacing the RunLLM widget that was removed in #67092 when that service reached end-of-life. The docs currently have no assistant.

## Claims

- Add `docs/mkdocs/javascript/ask_ai_widget.js`, a 15-line loader that injects the widget script on every docs page, and register it in `extra_javascript` in `mkdocs.yaml`.
- Same placement and shortcut as the old widget: bottom-right launcher, 120px up so it clears the version selector, opened with Cmd/Ctrl+J.
- The assistant answers from the vLLM docs (stable and latest), the blog, recipes.vllm.ai and GitHub issues / PRs / code under `vllm-project/`, and links every source it used.
- No change to the docs build, its dependencies or any other docs script.

## Validation

Not duplicating existing work: no open PR or issue adds a docs assistant (searched open PRs for "docs widget", "Ask AI", "RunLLM", "docs assistant", `run_llm_widget`; the only related PRs are #6857, which added the RunLLM widget, and #67092, which removed it).

Commands run:

- `pre-commit run` on the two changed files: passed.
- `node --check docs/mkdocs/javascript/ask_ai_widget.js`: passed.
- Parsed `mkdocs.yaml` with PyYAML (tolerating the mkdocs-specific tags): `extra_javascript` lists the new file first, the other five entries unchanged.

The loader was exercised on the live site rather than in a local build: the exact file from this PR was run in a browser against `https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/` before the page's own scripts, so `DOMContentLoaded` fires as it would on the built site. Checked with Chrome at 1440x900 and 390x780, light and dark scheme:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Script tag is created with the six attributes from the loader | pass |
| Launcher is visible bottom-right and overlaps no other fixed element (version selector, back-to-top) | pass, desktop and phone |
| Cmd/Ctrl+J opens the dialog | pass |
| Dialog background equals the page background in the `default` and `slate` schemes | pass |
| A question is answered cross-origin with linked sources | pass |
| Escape closes the dialog | pass |
| The widget is still there after an instant-navigation page change | pass |
| No uncaught page errors | pass |

A full `mkdocs build` was not run locally; the docs CI build covers that. The change adds one static file and one list entry.

## Details

**What loads.** One script from `https://vllm-docs-qa.vercel.app/widget.js`. It is dependency-free, renders inside a shadow root so it neither inherits nor leaks styles, and takes its colours from the Material theme variables. It sets no cookies; the conversation id lives in `sessionStorage` for the tab.

**Who runs it and what it receives.** The service is built and operated by Inferact. A question, any screenshot the reader attaches, and the URL of the docs page it was asked from are sent to that service, and from there to an LLM endpoint. Questions and answers are stored to keep the conversation and for quality review, with API keys, tokens and e-mail addresses redacted first; the service stores no account, name or IP address. Attached images are read once and not stored.

**Tradeoffs and limitations.**

- This is a third-party script on every docs page, loaded from a mutable URL, the same trust model as the RunLLM widget before it and as `reo.js` today. The dependency-pinning rules cover pip and GitHub Actions, not docs scripts, so nothing enforces a pin here.
- The script is served from a `vercel.app` address. A project domain would be a better long-term home and would need a one-line follow-up here.
- Answers are generated by a model and can be wrong; the dialog says so and links its sources.
- Rate limiting on the service is per instance today, and there is no automated answer-quality gate in this repository: quality is evaluated in the service's own repository.

AI assistance was used to write the loader, run the checks above and draft this description.
